Stage 3 · Grammar

The -ing form

English turns a verb into a noun by adding -ing. The only question is what comes before it.

Read these four sentences.
  • Cooking is the thing I do when I want to stop thinking.
  • I am interested in learning how other people eat.
  • I gave up eating meat two years ago.
  • I want to try it once before I decide.
Look at the word immediately before each -ing form. Which sentence is the odd one out, and why?
Where the -ing form goes
The choiceExampleWhy
As the subjectCooking is my way to relax.the activity is the topic of the sentence
As the objectI love trying new food.after love, like, enjoy, hate, don’t mind recycled
After a prepositionI am interested in learning to bake.in, at, about, of, on, after, before, without
After certain verbsI gave up eating meat.give up, keep, finish, avoid, suggest, start, stop
As an adjectiveboiled noodles · cooking oilthe form describes the noun
NOT hereI want to try it.  I decided to stop.want, would like, decide, hope, need take to + verb
Now choose the correct form. Look at the word before the gap first.
1She is good at ____ bread.
2I would like ____ your tagine one day.
3____ is cheaper than eating out.
4He kept ____ the sauce until it was thick.
5We decided ____ the meat out.
6She left without ____ anything.

FORM. verb + -ing. Doubling and dropping still apply: stop → stopping, bake → baking, lie → lying.

USE. The -ing form is the verb behaving like a noun. It can be the subject (Cooking is…), it follows a preposition (interested in learning), and it follows a fixed list of verbs (give up, keep, avoid, finish, suggest).

Not “I am interested to learn”, not “I gave up to eat meat”, not “To cook is my hobby” in everyday speech.

Next lesson the -ing form comes back inside the passive: the noodles are boiled before serving.

FORM. verb + -ing. Three spelling rules: drop a final silent -e (bake → baking); double a final consonant after one short vowel (stop → stopping, cut → cutting); -ie becomes -y (lie → lying).

USE 1 — the subject. When you want to talk about an activity itself, put it at the front with -ing: Cooking takes time. Eating alone is not the same. English can also say To cook takes time, but almost nobody does outside formal writing.

USE 2 — after a preposition. This is the rule that catches learners. After in, at, about, of, on, for, after, before, without the next verb is always -ing: interested in learning, good at baking, tired of cooking, before going out. Remember: to is sometimes a preposition too — I look forward to eating there, not to eat.

USE 3 — after certain verbs. A fixed group: give up, keep, finish, avoid, suggest, mind, practise, enjoy, start, stop. And a second group takes to + verb instead: want, would like, decide, hope, need, promise, agree. There is no rule — these are learned as pairs with their verb.

The three mistakes to watch: “I am interested to learn” (preposition, so -ing) · “I gave up to eat meat” (give up takes -ing) · “I enjoy to cook” (enjoy takes -ing).

The -ing form returns in Lesson 2 of this unit inside passive descriptions (the noodles are boiled before serving), and again in Unit 12 with the infinitive (my job is to find…).

Full grammar reference — Uses of the -ing form

Form

As the subjectCooking is my favourite way to relax.
After a prepositionI’m interested in learning more. · instead of buying it
After certain verbsenjoy · give up · avoid · keep · practise · mind · suggest
After go for activitiesgo swimming · go shopping · go camping
In a continuous tenseShe is cooking now. (a different job for the same form)

Spelling and sound

make → making · sit → sitting · lie → lying · travel → travelling.

When and why we use it

  • When a verb is used as the name of an activity, English puts it in the -ing form.
  • A subject in -ing takes a singular verb: Cooking is relaxing.
  • The rule after prepositions has no exceptions: before leaving, after eating, without asking.
  • To is sometimes a preposition, and then it also takes -ing: I’m looking forward to seeing you.

Signal words

interested in · good at · tired of · instead of · before / after · without

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • Cook is my hobby. → Cooking is my hobby.The activity takes -ing.
  • I’m interested in learn. → … interested in learning.After a preposition.
  • Cooking are relaxing. → Cooking is relaxing.Singular verb.
  • I look forward to see you. → I look forward to seeing you.To is a preposition here.

Don’t confuse it with

-ing as a name of an activity (Swimming is good for you) against -ing in a tense (She is swimming now). Same form, different job.

Stage 5 · Main input

Why two people can eat the same thing and disagree completely.

Before you read: some people love very bitter food and some cannot swallow it.

What do you think the main reason is? Choose one, then read and find out.

No right answer yet. This is your prediction.

A question of taste

Written for this course · A2

Two people sit down to the same plate of food. One eats happily; the other cannot finish it. Scientists now think that liking or disliking a food is not one thing but three.

What you are born with. Your tongue is covered with taste buds, and people do not have the same number of them. Researchers at the Monell Chemical Senses Center describe a group they call “supertasters”: roughly a quarter of people, who have far more taste buds than average. For them a plain green vegetable is not plain at all — it is strongly bitter, and a very sour or spicy dish can be painful. Avoiding spinach, then, is not fussiness. It is information.

What you grow up with. Babies already know the flavours their mother ate, because those flavours reach them before birth. After that, the rule is simple: the more often a child meets a food, the more likely they are to accept it. Studies suggest it takes eight to ten tastes, not one: a herb or a spice that is strange at four is ordinary at six. Giving up after the second refusal is the mistake most parents make.

What it feels like. Texture decides more than people admit. Many children who happily eat a boiled carrot will refuse the same carrot raw, and many adults who like the flavour of an olive still cannot eat one. It is not the taste. It is the mouth.

So the next time somebody leaves something on the plate, the answer is probably not that they are being polite about your cooking.

Sources. Taste-bud variation and the supertaster group: Monell Chemical Senses Center · flavour learning before birth and repeated exposure: published infant-feeding research summarised by the British Nutrition Foundation · texture and food refusal: BBC Future. Written for this course; no source text is reproduced.
